[LLM] payload.bin written under node_modules by node process Installation High
Detects the Gen-1 stager dropping the ~195 KB Bun-compiled second-stage binary as payload.bin inside the package install directory beneath node_modules. The combination of filename, parent directory, and node initiating process is article-specific and very high fidelity. Rationale: Block 2 in the article literally is this detection — payload.bin name + node_modules path + node initiator is exactly the Gen-1 drop. Filename is too generic on its own (any backup or game asset could be called payload.bin) but combined with node_modules + node initiator the FP rate collapses.
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "payload.bin"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "npx.cmd", "npx.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "payload.bin"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "npm", "npx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound HTTP beacon to vpmdhaj C2 (aab.sportsontheweb.net) Command & Control High
Detects the Gen-1 stager's HTTP C2 beacon and stage-2 download from the vpmdhaj-controlled domain. Scopes the connection on the C2 hostname plus node as the initiating process so non-developer traffic is excluded. Rationale: aab.sportsontheweb.net is the only IOC the article surfaces as a Gen-1 C2 host. Scoping on the FQDN (rather than the X-Supply header, which is not consistently captured in standard CEF / ASIM columns) gives a clean, high-fidelity detection that survives across DNS, proxy, and EDR network telemetry.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "aab.sportsontheweb.net"
   or RemoteUrl endswith "sportsontheweb.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Host = "aab.sportsontheweb.net";
(union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where DestinationHostName has C2Host
          or RequestURL has C2Host
          or DestinationDnsDomain has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName,
               RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, RequestMethod,
               SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where Url has C2Host or DstHostname has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname,
               Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpMethod,
               HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpResponseBodyBytes, EventProduct),
  (DnsEvents
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where Name has C2Host
     | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] __DAEMONIZED=1 environment marker on spawned process Installation High
Detects the vpmdhaj stage-2 binary's self-re-entry guard, which sets __DAEMONIZED=1 in the environment of the detached child to avoid double-spawning. This env-var name is unique to this campaign per Microsoft's writeup. Rationale: Block 3 in the article — the __DAEMONIZED=1 string is a unique campaign artifact called out explicitly in Microsoft's writeup as the re-entry guard. The literal string is not a known legitimate environment variable in any common runtime so single-string match is sufficient.
ATT&CKT1543 T1564
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or AdditionalFields has "__DAEMONIZED"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "__DAEMONIZED=1"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cloud metadata service hit (IMDSv2 / ECS) from node process under node_modules Actions on Objectives High
Detects the stage-2 credential harvester's queries against AWS Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) and ECS task-role metadata (169.254.170.2) when the originating process is node — particularly when launched from a node_modules path. Pairs the EDR-side metadata fetch with the CloudTrail-side STS/SecretsManager fan-out for correlation. Rationale: 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2) and 169.254.170.2 (ECS task role) are the exact metadata endpoints the article names. Pairing the link-local destination with a node/bun initiating process is the article-specific anchor; the CloudTrail companion query catches the fan-out across 16+ regions (GetCallerIdentity → AssumeRole → ListSecrets/GetSecretValue) called out as a defining behaviour of the stage-2 harvester.
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1528 T1555.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "bun.exe", "bun")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "node_modules"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall.js", "setup.mjs", "opensearch_init.js", "ai_init.js", "payload.bin")
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ParentCmds = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5),
            ParentPaths = make_set(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, 5)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "169.254.170.2")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: AWS IMDSv2 / ECS Metadata Hit From Node
id: a7c91d54-2f8e-4b3a-9c1d-5e8f7a3b6c20
description: Detects an outbound connection to the AWS instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-role metadata endpoint (169.254.170.2) initiated by a node / bun process — a signature of the vpmdhaj stage-2 credential harvester.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/typosquatted-npm-packages-used-steal-cloud-ci-cd-secrets/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.005
  - attack.t1555.006
logsource:
  category: network_connection
selection_ip:
  DestinationIp:
    - '169.254.169.254'
    - '169.254.170.2'
selection_proc:
  Image|endswith:
    - '\node.exe'
    - '\bun.exe'
    - '/node'
    - '/bun'
condition: selection_ip and selection_proc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(169.254.169.254 OR 169.254.170.2) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\bun.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^169\.254\.(169\.254|170\.2)$/
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\node\.exe|\\bun\.exe|\/node|\/bun)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, awsRegion
| filter eventName in ["GetCallerIdentity", "AssumeRole", "ListSecrets", "GetSecretValue"]
  and userIdentity.type in ["AssumedRole", "IAMUser", "WebIdentityUser"]
  and (userAgent like /aws-sdk-js/i or userAgent like /node/i or userAgent like /Bun/i)
| stats count() as call_count,
        count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_events,
        count_distinct(awsRegion) as distinct_regions,
        earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen,
        latest(@timestamp) as last_seen
        by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress
| filter distinct_regions >= 5 and distinct_events >= 2
| sort call_count desc

[LLM] Bun runtime download from github.com/oven-sh during npm install (Gen-2 loader) Delivery Medium
Detects the Gen-2 stager's hallmark: an npm-driven node process fetching a legitimate Bun runtime release (v1.3.13) directly from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases as a loader for the bundled stage-2 payload. The combination of source (npm install) + destination (oven-sh/bun release asset) is the article-specific signal. Rationale: The article names github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases v1.3.13 as the legitimate-but-abused payload host for the Gen-2 setup.mjs loader. github.com is trusted egress so destination alone is too noisy; pairing it with a node/npm initiating process during install lifecycle bounds the FP rate to actual Bun adopters.
ATT&CKT1105 T1218
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com" and RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "npx.cmd")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs", "preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install", "node_modules")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "github.com" and Url has "oven-sh/bun"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "npm", "npx")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs", "preinstall", "postinstall", "npm install", "node_modules")
  ) on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1)) <= 300
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime Pulled From GitHub During npm Install

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PhantomMail: Ukrainian-themed ZIP/RAR delivered via Google Drive or 4sync links · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PhantomClick: browser → mshta/powershell/cmd within 60s of fake Cloudflare/Zoom/LAPAS lure · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GreyVibe: RDP enablement via fDenyTSConnections=0 + firewall by PowerShell RAT
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PowerShell.exe sustained beaconing to uncategorized web endpoint (LegionRelay/PhantomRelay C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LegionRelay browser credential theft from Chromium/Firefox Login Data by PowerShell · [LLM] LegionRelay Telegram / WhatsApp messenger store exfiltration · [LLM] GreyVibe cryptocurrency miner deployment via PowerShell RAT
[LLM] PhantomMail: Ukrainian-themed ZIP/RAR delivered via Google Drive or 4sync links Delivery Medium
Hunts GreyVibe's PhantomMail vector: spear-phishing emails with ZIP/RAR attachments or body links to Google Drive / 4sync, themed against Ukrainian gov, emergency, telecom or energy entities. Pivots on archive attachments plus the two specific cloud-storage URL families called out by WithSecure. Rationale: Anchors on WithSecure-stated PhantomMail strings: ZIP/RAR archives, Google Drive and 4sync links, and Ukrainian gov/emergency/telecom/energy lure impersonation. Mail-only signal so endpoint queries are deferred to the execution UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002

[LLM] PhantomClick: browser → mshta/powershell/cmd within 60s of fake Cloudflare/Zoom/LAPAS lure Exploitation High
Hunts the PhantomClick ClickFix flow: victim visits a fake Zoom or LAPAS site, the page displays a fake Cloudflare verification, and the user pastes a self-infecting command. Pivots on a browser parent spawning interpreter children within seconds, with the cmdline carrying ClickFix-style payload markers. Rationale: Maps directly to WithSecure's PhantomClick description: fake Cloudflare/Zoom/LAPAS verification leading users to paste self-infecting commands. Combines browser parent + interpreter child + ClickFix telltale strings (Cloudflare, ray-id, captcha, lapas, Verify you are human). Cross-checked against MITRE T1204.001 and recurring ClickFix Sigma rules to ensure novelty. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001 T1059.003

SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") | where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where CommandLine has_any ("I am not a robot","Cloudflare","ray-id","verification","captcha","zoom","lapas","FromBase64String","IEX","Invoke-Expression","irm ","mshta http","curl http","Verify you are human") | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] LegionRelay browser credential theft from Chromium/Firefox Login Data by PowerShell Actions on Objectives High
Hunts LegionRelay's browser credential-theft module: PowerShell or other non-browser processes reading Chromium 'Login Data' / 'Local State' and Firefox 'logins.json' / 'key4.db'. Article calls out browser credential theft as a built-in capability of the LegionRelay RAT. Rationale: WithSecure says LegionRelay 'supports … browser credential theft'. Targets the universal artefact paths of the Chromium and Firefox credential vaults, gated on a non-browser scripting-host parent — the article calls out LegionRelay as a PowerShell-based RAT. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","Cookies","Web Data") | where FolderPath has_any ("\\Google\\Chrome\\","\\Microsoft\\Edge\\","\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\","\\BraveSoftware\\","\\Opera Software\\") | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","explorer.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","backup.exe") | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","Cookies","Web Data") | where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\Google\\Chrome\\","\\Microsoft\\Edge\\","\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\","\\BraveSoftware\\","\\Opera Software\\") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] LegionRelay Telegram / WhatsApp messenger store exfiltration Actions on Objectives High
Hunts LegionRelay's messenger exfiltration capability: non-Telegram / non-WhatsApp processes reading Telegram Desktop's tdata vault or WhatsApp's Local Storage / msgstore. Article explicitly names Telegram and WhatsApp data exfiltration as core LegionRelay functionality. Rationale: WithSecure explicitly says LegionRelay supports 'Telegram and WhatsApp data exfiltration'. Anchors on the canonical Telegram tdata folder and WhatsApp Desktop Local Storage/IndexedDB layout, gated on non-messenger scripting/archiver parent to keep FP rate low. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/

ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\Telegram Desktop\\tdata\\","\\WhatsApp\\Local Storage\\","\\WhatsApp\\IndexedDB\\") or TargetFileName in~ ("key_datas","msgstore.db") | where ActingProcessName !has_any ("telegram.exe","whatsapp.exe") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","7z.exe","winrar.exe") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GreyVibe: RDP enablement via fDenyTSConnections=0 + firewall by PowerShell RAT Installation High
Hunts LegionRelay's 'RDP access setup' capability: PowerShell or cmd flipping fDenyTSConnections to 0, enabling UserAuthentication, or opening the RDP firewall rule. Article explicitly calls out RDP access setup as a LegionRelay function and the attacker uses PowerShell-based RATs. Rationale: WithSecure: 'LegionRelay supports … RDP access setup.' Anchors on the canonical Windows knobs an attacker has to flip to enable RDP on a previously-disabled host: fDenyTSConnections=0 registry value, UserAuthentication relax, and the RemoteDesktop firewall group. Gated on a scripting-host parent because the article describes the actor as PowerShell-based. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/004/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1112 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Processes

let RegFlip = ImRegistryEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where (RegistryKey has "\\Terminal Server" and RegistryValue == "fDenyTSConnections" and RegistryValueData == "0") or (RegistryKey has "\\WinStations\\RDP-Tcp" and RegistryValue == "UserAuthentication") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","reg.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData; let CmdFlip = SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","netsh.exe","reg.exe") | where CommandLine has_any ("fDenyTSConnections","Enable-NetFirewallRule","netsh advfirewall","Set-ItemProperty") | where CommandLine has_any ("Terminal Server","RemoteDesktop","TermService","RDP-Tcp","UserAuthentication") | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine; union RegFlip, CmdFlip | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PowerShell.exe sustained beaconing to uncategorized web endpoint (LegionRelay/PhantomRelay C2) Command & Control Medium
Hunts the LegionRelay/PhantomRelay PowerShell RAT C2 pattern: powershell.exe making repeated outbound HTTPS connections to a single rare external endpoint with no parent browser. Article describes both RATs as PowerShell-based with web C2 (UTC+3 panels, shared PrincessClub/DroneLink infra). Rationale: Both LegionRelay and PhantomRelay are described as PowerShell RATs and the C2 servers are on UTC+3 with web panels. Threshold + low-cardinality destination expresses 'beaconing' rather than one-shot egress. Doesn't reference specific IOCs from the article on purpose — actor rotates infra — but constrains pivot to powershell.exe initiated egress. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102

[LLM] GreyVibe cryptocurrency miner deployment via PowerShell RAT Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the cryptominer impact tail of the GreyVibe campaign: known miner binaries (xmrig, ethminer, t-rex, lolMiner) or Stratum protocol egress from victim machines. Article explicitly notes a cryptocurrency miner was deployed on some victim machines. Rationale: WithSecure: 'a cryptocurrency miner was deployed on some victim machines.' Anchors on the well-known XMRig/RandomX family + Stratum protocol strings + canonical mining pool ports (3333/4444/5555/7777/14444) and pool domains. Article didn't ship a specific miner SHA so we rely on family-level indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1496/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/greyvibe-hackers-use-chatgpt-gemini-to-power-cyberattacks/
ATT&CKT1496

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] BTMOB phishing/C2 domain lookup: arbsniper.com · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 observed on managed device · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to known infrastructure IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to known infrastructure IPs Command & Control High
Detects any corporate-network egress to the BTMOB RAT command-and-control IP set published by ESET and Cyble. BTMOB uses WebSocket-based C2 on these endpoints; a single connection from a managed Android (or any) device is high-fidelity since these IPs serve no legitimate enterprise purpose. Rationale: Direct IOC match against the 8 C2 IPs the article lists. Cross-checked with ESET WeLiveSecurity BTMOB write-up and Cyble's Feb-2025 BTMOB 2.5 analysis — same infrastructure cluster, WebSocket C2 protocol — so these IPs aren't fronting CDNs or shared hosting most enterprises would naturally touch. Defender for Endpoint covers Android too, so DeviceNetworkEvents surfaces the BYOD/MDM-enrolled phone egress as well as desktop hits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1437.001

[LLM] BTMOB phishing/C2 domain lookup: arbsniper.com Delivery High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP/S contact with arbsniper.com, the clearnet front for the BTMOB malware-as-a-service identified by ESET. The domain hosts the operator portal and BTMOB lure infrastructure; any enterprise device touching it is either a victim of a phishing redirect or an operator/researcher pivot. Rationale: Single high-confidence domain published in the BleepingComputer article and confirmed as the BTMOB operator portal in ESET's WeLiveSecurity write-up. Domain is exclusive to the MaaS operation — no shared SaaS hosting risk. Covers DNS-layer hits (DnsEvents / ImDnsActivity), egress proxy hits, and Defender's UrlClickEvents so we catch a user clicking the phishing URL out of email as well as on-device beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/

[LLM] BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 observed on managed device Installation High
Detects file-write, download, or attachment events matching the 8 BTMOB SHA256 hashes published by ESET. Covers BYOD/MDM-enrolled Android endpoints, corporate Windows hosts that may have been used to sideload an APK to a phone via USB, and email attachment scanning. Rationale: Exact-hash IOC match — zero-FP by construction once cross-checked against an authoritative source. Hashes pulled straight from BleepingComputer / ESET write-up and corroborated against Cyble's BTMOB 2.5 sample set. Defender for Endpoint covers Android, so DeviceFileEvents picks up APK drops on enrolled phones; EmailAttachmentInfo covers the email-delivery vector; AlertEvidence catches AV/MDE detonation hits that already triggered. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/ • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://forum.eset.com/topic/49121-btmob-a-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-into-android-devices

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DNS/HTTP traffic to Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains (2026 World Cup fraud) · [LLM] Browser navigation to FIFA-themed look-alike hostname (typosquat pattern hunt) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Ghost Stadium FIFA fraud staging IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Risky AAD sign-in after user contact with FIFA typosquat phishing portal
[LLM] DNS/HTTP traffic to Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains (2026 World Cup fraud) Delivery High
Hunts for endpoint resolution or HTTP requests to the eight FIFA look-alike domains called out in the FBI 2026 World Cup PSA and Group-IB's Ghost Stadium reporting. High-fidelity because these hostnames have no legitimate business use. Rationale: Uses the eight specific typosquat hostnames named by the FBI PSA and the Group-IB Ghost Stadium report. Hostnames have no legitimate business use; first-touch is high-fidelity for both DNS and proxy logs.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1189 T1583.001

let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (TyposquatDomains)

let ClickHits = UrlClickEvents

[LLM] Outbound connection to Ghost Stadium FIFA fraud staging IPs Command & Control High
Alerts when any internal host establishes an outbound connection to the eight staging IPs that host the cloned FIFA ticketing/employment/merchandise portals. Catches cases where the typosquat domain was bypassed via direct link, URL shortener, or DNS-over-HTTPS resolution that escaped DNS-tier visibility. Rationale: Targets the eight staging IPs explicitly pre-extracted from the FBI PSA / Group-IB infrastructure tracking. IP-tier detection catches victims who reach the cloned portals via shortened URLs or DoH that bypass DNS visibility.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (StagingIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (StagingIPs) or SourceIP in (StagingIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Browser navigation to FIFA-themed look-alike hostname (typosquat pattern hunt) Delivery Medium
Hunting query that surfaces browser traffic to any domain matching the FIFA typosquat pattern family (extra/missing letters, hyphenated subbrands like -hiring/-hr/-careerhub/-ticket, doubled-W prefixes) excluding the legitimate fifa.com/fifa.org. Designed to catch the long tail of the 300+ Ghost Stadium domains beyond the eight in the FBI PSA. Rationale: Article + Group-IB attribution names 300+ Ghost Stadium domains, only 8 of which are pre-extracted. The regex covers the family of typosquat patterns described (homoglyph: fiffa/filfa/f1fa, doubled-W: wvvw-/ww-, sub-brand hyphens: -hiring/-hr/-ticket/-careerhub) while explicitly excluding genuine fifa.com/fifa.org.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesWeb
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Hostname = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl)["Host"]))
| where Hostname matches regex @"(fiff[ai]|filfa|f1fa|fifaa|wvvw-?fifa|ww-?fifa|fifa-?(hiring|hr|ticket|tickets|careers?|careerhub|jobs|hospitality|online|com|worldcup|world-cup|2026|store|merch|panini))"
| where Hostname != "fifa.com" and Hostname != "fifa.org" and Hostname !endswith ".fifa.com" and Hostname !endswith ".fifa.org"
| summarize HitCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Devices=dcount(DeviceName), Users=dcount(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn), SampleUrls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 5) by Hostname
| order by FirstSeen desc
let LookalikeRegex = @"(?i)(fiff[ai]|filfa|f1fa|fifaa|wvvw-?fifa|ww-?fifa|fifa-?(hiring|hr|ticket|tickets|careers?|careerhub|jobs|hospitality|online|com|worldcup|world-cup|2026|store|merch|panini))";
union
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName matches regex LookalikeRegex or RequestURL matches regex LookalikeRegex | extend Host=tolower(DestinationHostName) | where Host != "fifa.com" and Host != "fifa.org" and Host !endswith ".fifa.com" and Host !endswith ".fifa.org" | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, Host, RequestURL, Source="Proxy"),
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name matches regex LookalikeRegex | extend Host=tolower(Name) | where Host != "fifa.com" and Host != "fifa.org" and Host !endswith ".fifa.com" and Host !endswith ".fifa.org" | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=ClientIP, SourceUserName="", Host, RequestURL="", Source="DNS")
| summarize HitCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Sources=dcount(SourceIP) by Host
| order by FirstSeen desc
(@http.url_details.host:*fifa* OR @network.destination.domain:*fifa* OR @dns.question.name:*fifa*) AND -@http.url_details.host:(fifa.com OR www.fifa.com OR fifa.org OR www.fifa.org) AND -@network.destination.domain:(fifa.com OR www.fifa.com OR fifa.org OR www.fifa.org) AND -@dns.question.name:(fifa.com OR www.fifa.com OR fifa.org OR www.fifa.org)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| regex("(fiff[ai]|filfa|f1fa|fifaa|wvvw-?fifa|ww-?fifa|fifa-?(hiring|hr|ticket|tickets|careers?|careerhub|jobs|hospitality|online|com|worldcup|world-cup|2026|store|merch|panini))", field=DomainName, flags="i")
| DomainName!=/^(www\.)?fifa\.(com|org)$/i
| groupBy([DomainName], function={ count() | dcount(field=aid, as=hosts) | min(_time, as=firstSeen) })

[LLM] Risky AAD sign-in after user contact with FIFA typosquat phishing portal Actions on Objectives Medium
Correlates users who visited any of the Ghost Stadium FIFA typosquat domains with subsequent risky/anomalous Entra ID sign-ins within 7 days. Targets the post-credential-submission account-takeover pivot described in the article ('create fraudulent accounts, commit identity theft'). Rationale: The article explicitly states the harvested PII/credentials are used 'to create fraudulent accounts, commit identity theft'. Joining typosquat visitors against subsequent risky AAD sign-ins is the only way to spot the account-takeover step. The 7-day delay window covers actor lag between data collection and credential reuse.
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication Web
let TyposquatDomains = dynamic(["fiffa.com","jobs-fifa.com","fifa-hiring.com","filfa.org","wvvw-fifa.com","ww-fifa.com","fifa-hr.com","fifa-careerhub.com"]);
let Visitors = union
    (DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (TyposquatDomains) | where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn) | project VisitTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn=tolower(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn), DeviceName, VisitedHost=RemoteUrl),
    (UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where Url has_any (TyposquatDomains) | where isnotempty(AccountUpn) | project VisitTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn=tolower(AccountUpn), DeviceName="", VisitedHost=Url);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("medium","high") or RiskLevelAggregated in ("medium","high") or RiskState in ("atRisk","confirmedCompromised")
| extend AccountUpn=tolower(AccountUpn)
| join kind=inner Visitors on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (VisitTime .. VisitTime + 7d)
| extend DelayHours = datetime_diff('hour', Timestamp, VisitTime)
| project SignInTime=Timestamp, VisitTime, DelayHours, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, Application, VisitedHost, DeviceName
| order by SignInTime desc
let TyposquatDomains = dynamic(["fiffa.com","jobs-fifa.com","fifa-hiring.com","filfa.org","wvvw-fifa.com","ww-fifa.com","fifa-hr.com","fifa-careerhub.com"]);
let Visitors = union
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where (RequestURL has_any (TyposquatDomains)) or (DestinationHostName has_any (TyposquatDomains)) | where isnotempty(SourceUserName) | project VisitTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName=tolower(SourceUserName), VisitedHost=coalesce(DestinationHostName,RequestURL)),
    (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where csReferer has_any (TyposquatDomains) | where isnotempty(csUserName) | project VisitTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName=tolower(csUserName), VisitedHost=csReferer);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("medium","high") or RiskLevelAggregated in ("medium","high") or RiskState in ("atRisk","confirmedCompromised")
| extend UserPrincipalName=tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| join kind=inner Visitors on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (VisitTime .. VisitTime + 7d)
| extend DelayHours = datetime_diff('hour', TimeGenerated, VisitTime)
| project SignInTime=TimeGenerated, VisitTime, DelayHours, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, AppDisplayName, VisitedHost
| order by SignInTime desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(fiffa\.com|jobs-fifa\.com|fifa-hiring\.com|filfa\.org|wvvw-fifa\.com|ww-fifa\.com|fifa-hr\.com|fifa-careerhub\.com)$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog RiskLevel=/medium|high/i EventResult=success}, field=[aid], include=[UserPrincipal, RemoteIp, RiskLevel, _time])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserPrincipal, DomainName, RiskLevel], function=count())
